common_name: Green Rose (Viridiflora, Novelty Antique China Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Green Rose is an antique China rose sport first documented in the 1830s-1850s whose blooms are made entirely of sepal-like green bracts instead of colored petals, and it shares the exceptional heat and disease tolerance of other China roses, making it a reliable curiosity for Gulf South gardens.

directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained soil, spacing plants 2-3 feet apart. Green Rose, also sold as Viridiflora, is one of the odder curiosities in the rose world: a China rose sport whose flowers never develop true petals, instead producing dense clusters of jagged, sepal-like bracts that open bright green and age to a rusty maroon-bronze, giving the plant an unusual, almost floral-arrangement look rather than typical rose color. It has no traditional fragrance but is a favorite of flower arrangers for its novelty and long vase life. Like other China roses it blooms nearly continuously from spring through frost and shares their outstanding tolerance for heat, humidity, and blackspot, needing little spraying or care in the Gulf South. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove dead wood, and expect curious questions from visitors who assume the buds simply haven't opened yet.
sources: The Antique Rose Emporium — Green Rose variety notes
American Rose Society — China Rose Class Descriptions

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Ducher is an 1869 French China rose noted for being one of the hardiest and most cold-tolerant of the China class, while still carrying the class's excellent heat and humidity tolerance for the Gulf South.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, compost-enriched soil, spacing plants 2-3 feet apart. Introduced in France in 1869, Ducher is a compact China rose bearing clusters of fragrant, fully double, creamy-white blooms tinged with pale pink at the center, set against small, dark, glossy foliage. It is considered one of the most cold-hardy roses in the China class, extending its usefulness slightly beyond the warmest zones where most Chinas thrive, while still carrying their signature nonstop bloom cycle and strong resistance to blackspot and powdery mildew in humid climates. The compact, rounded shrub suits borders, low hedges, and container culture. Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead or crossing wood; deadhead spent blooms to encourage the next flush, though the plant reblooms readily even without deadheading.

common_name: Souvenir de la Malmaison Rose (Classic 1843 Bourbon Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall in a site with excellent air circulation; Souvenir de la Malmaison is an 1843 Bourbon rose named for Empress Josephine's garden and prized for huge, quartered, intensely fragrant blooms, though its densely petaled flowers can ball and fail to open in prolonged Gulf Coast humidity, so afternoon shade and open air movement help performance.

directions: Plant in full sun with excellent air circulation in well-drained, fertile soil, spacing plants 3-4 feet apart. Introduced in France in 1843 and named for the rose garden of Empress Josephine at Château de Malmaison, this Bourbon rose is famous for enormous, flat, quartered blooms in soft blush-pink packed with dozens of petals and a rich, classic old-rose fragrance considered among the finest of any rose. It blooms in flushes from spring through fall on a compact, sturdy shrub, but in the humid Gulf South its densely petaled blooms can 'ball' — swelling with trapped moisture and failing to open — so siting it where morning sun dries the foliage quickly and air moves freely improves bloom quality. It is more disease-resistant than most Bourbons but still benefits from being kept away from overhead irrigation. Prune lightly after each bloom flush to remove spent flowers and shape the plant, and avoid heavy pruning, which reduces flowering.

common_name: Rêve d'Or Rose (Golden Noisette Climbing Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall at the base of a trellis, arbor, or fence; Rêve d'Or is an 1869 Noisette climber descended from roses bred in Charleston, South Carolina, and Noisettes as a class are exceptionally well adapted to the heat and humidity of the Gulf South.

directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained, fertile soil at the base of a sturdy support, allowing 5-8 feet for its mature spread. Introduced in France in 1869, Rêve d'Or ('dream of gold') is a Noisette climbing rose bearing large, fully double, buff-yellow to apricot blooms with a fruity tea fragrance against handsome, glossy, almost evergreen foliage. The Noisette class originated in Charleston, South Carolina, in the early 1800s from roses bred specifically to handle Southern heat and humidity, and Rêve d'Or carries that heritage, blooming repeatedly from spring through fall with strong disease resistance and minimal care once established. Train the long, relatively thornless canes horizontally along a fence or arbor to encourage the most flowers, since roses bloom more heavily from canes trained near-horizontal than from those left to grow straight up. Prune lightly after the main spring flush to remove spent wood and maintain the desired shape, saving hard structural pruning for full dormancy in winter.
